record.original_question: Does universal gravitational coupling require introducing Newton's constant G as a fundamental coupling in classical gravity, or can a gravitational theory provide universal coupling without fundamental G? In particular, can the role played by G in Newton-Einstein gravity be replaced by source moments governed by a dimensionless conformal coupling while still reproducing the observed weak-gravity Newtonian phenomenology?

evidence.quote: Thus we need to ask whether the potential really is 1/r on much larger distance scales, and whether universal coupling actually necessitates the introduction of the fundamental constant G in the first place.
Thus our theory meets Newton’s final demand, namely that gravity be universally coupled; and interestingly we see that the theory is able to do so without the need to introduce G at all.

Since in the standard theory G is not independently measurable anyway as it only ever appears in the product MG (its canonically quoted value just represents the choice of units in which to measure mass), we see, that despite its longevity, Newton’s constant may not actually play any fundamental role in physics at all.
This of course would be a severe problem for the Einstein-Hilbert action since it gives fundamental status to G.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a classical relativistic theory of gravity in which the gravitational field is universally coupled to matter, in the sense that all test bodies fall along the same trajectories in a given external gravitational field (the weak equivalence principle), and in which, in the weak-field, slow-motion regime, the theory reproduces Newtonian phenomenology — in particular, a static, spherically symmetric source produces an attractive 1/r potential at laboratory and solar-system scales.

In the standard Newton–Einstein formulation, this is achieved by introducing a dimensionful fundamental coupling constant G (Newton's constant), appearing in the Einstein–Hilbert action S = (1/16πG) ∫ R √(−g) d⁴x and entering the matter–gravity coupling through the combination MG.

Question: Is the introduction of a dimensionful fundamental coupling G logically necessary in any classical gravitational theory that exhibits universal coupling and reproduces Newtonian weak-field phenomenology? Equivalently, does there exist a classical gravitational theory — for example, one built from a dimensionless action with only dimensionless conformal couplings, in which the strength of the gravitational field produced by a source is set by moments (mass, size, internal structure) of the source rather than by a universal dimensionful constant — that (i) couples universally to matter, (ii) reproduces the observed 1/r Newtonian potential and its phenomenology in the appropriate regime, and (iii) contains no fundamental Newton constant G? If such a theory exists, characterize the mechanism by which source moments under a dimensionless conformal coupling can replicate the role conventionally played by G.
artifact.status_search_result: Within Mannheim's conformal gravity program, an affirmative construction has been proposed: gravity is sourced by dimensionless conformal couplings and source moments, so that the effective Newtonian coupling emerges without a fundamental dimensionful G. A 2022 EPL paper ("Conformal gravity: Newton's constant is not universal") develops exactly this viewpoint, arguing G is non-universal and emerges from source structure. However, whether such a theory fully reproduces all observed weak-field Newtonian phenomenology and whether G truly plays no fundamental role remain debated, with published critiques and replies. So the question is partially addressed within the conformal-gravity framework but not settled as a general theorem about classical gravity.

status_evidence.title: Conformal gravity: Newton's constant is not universal
status_evidence.snippet: Argues that in conformal gravity Newton's constant differs for different sources (e.g., neutron vs. proton) and is not a universal fundamental constant.
status_evidence.claim: A concrete realization in which G is not fundamental/universal has been proposed within conformal gravity.

status_evidence.title: Conformal gravity - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Conformal gravity uses dimensionless couplings; in contrast to conventional gravity G is not dimensionless and is replaced by dimensionless conformal couplings.
status_evidence.claim: Conformal gravity is built on dimensionless couplings, supporting the possibility of universal coupling without a fundamental G.

status_evidence.title: Comment on 'Problems with Mannheim's conformal gravity program'
status_evidence.snippet: Ongoing debate about whether conformal gravity reproduces standard Newtonian/weak-field phenomenology.
status_evidence.claim: The reproduction of full Newtonian phenomenology without fundamental G remains contested.
